title: Why credible bank resolution changes the capital the system needs
summary: Deputy Governor Dave Ramsden argues that the UK can calibrate capital requirements more proportionately because it has a credible way to deal with bank failure. A regime that imposes losses on investors rather than taxpayers can discipline excessive risk-taking before distress. If a firm still fails, preserving payments and credit services can reduce the duration and economic cost of the crisis. These two effects lower the amount of capital needed to protect the financial system in normal times. The argument is conditional on the authorities being able to execute a resolution under pressure. It is not a claim that every bank has excess capital or that a particular security offers an attractive spread (pp. 2–6).

The FPC's revised benchmark is around 13% of risk-weighted assets for system-wide Tier 1 requirements, down one percentage point. It covers aggregate requirements and buffers for major UK banks in a standard risk environment, including the UK countercyclical buffer at its neutral setting. A substantially larger number in the speech refers to a different exercise. Ramsden says the post-crisis framework, particularly credible resolution, reduces the appropriate benchmark by roughly five percentage points relative to a counterfactual. Without it, the latest recalibration might have been from 19% to 18%, all else equal. Chart 2 expresses the model's expected net macroeconomic benefit relative to the benchmark as a percentage of annual GDP. The cost rises sharply when capital is reduced in the scenario without effective resolution. The five-point comparison is model-dependent, and the assumed 60% reduction in the discounted cost of crises is an input from the study underlying the analysis (pp. 4–6, endnote 2).

Ramsden offers market evidence for the discipline channel. He cites an estimated bail-in premium of around 30–45 basis points for a sample of large UK banks, reduced rating-agency assumptions of government support for holding-company bondholders and evidence that risk pricing varies across firms. These observations support the idea that creditors take their loss exposure seriously. They are distinct from a forward-looking estimate of crisis costs. The government's £137 billion injection to stabilise financial firms during the global financial crisis measures public money injected. Chart 1 measures growth in output per hour, showing Britain's relatively weak performance in the decade after the crisis. Neither number identifies the incremental GDP benefit of the current regime (pp. 4–5).

The distribution of upfront financing costs depends on the likely resolution strategy. Firms subject to bail-in issue equity and subordinated liabilities capable of absorbing losses and recapitalising the bank while it restructures. UK-headquartered firms with a bail-in strategy held more than £430 billion of external MREL in aggregate at the third quarter of 2025. Under the January changes, the indicative asset range for considering resolution tools rises from £15–25 billion to £25–40 billion. The Bank will assess individual firms' suitability for transfer, and transfer firms no longer need MREL above minimum capital requirements. Several firms in the new range had already been assigned transfer strategies in December. An industry-funded recapitalisation mechanism creates another option for eligible smaller failures. The FSCS levy is subject to affordability. These changes shift the timing and allocation of costs; they do not remove losses from the system (pp. 7–9, Figure 1, endnotes 3–5).

Operational capability is the counterpart to lower upfront costs. The next major-bank assessment was expected to publish findings in summer 2027, testing how eight institutions would continue operating and prepare restructuring on realistic resolution timetables. The Bank expected an operational transfer guide covering rapid auctions and bidder selection, and an updated bail-in guide. Home and host authorities were rehearsing coordination through crisis management groups and exercises. The December increase in eligible deposit protection from £85,000 to £120,000 was another support for depositor confidence. Ramsden considered the main bank-resolution policy changes implemented, subject to unexpected developments, while identifying practical work still needed for central counterparty resolution (pp. 9–12).

Part of the risk has moved beyond banking. Non-bank financial institutions accounted for around half of financial assets globally and in the UK. Major UK banks' exposures to them, excluding derivatives, had risen from 17% of assets in 2018 to 21% in 2024. Chart 3 shows sectoral net gilt repo positions in pounds, with hedge fund borrowing much larger by November 2025. Net funding is a different measure from gross exposures or potential losses. A forced sale can transmit a liquidity shock through gilt and repo markets even where the originating fund falls outside the Bank's resolution remit. The contingent repo facility can provide liquidity against gilts to eligible, suitably regulated insurers, pension funds and LDI funds during severe dysfunction. It is not general insurance for hedge fund positions. Wider central clearing and minimum haircuts were being discussed. A planned system-wide exercise would examine private markets (pp. 12–14, Chart 3, endnote 7).

The speech also distinguishes proposed safeguards for systemic sterling stablecoins from existing bank arrangements. The consultation envisaged central bank deposit accounts, some short-dated gilt backing, statutory trusts and externally validated wind-down plans. Liquidity backstops and eventual insurance or statutory creditor preference were still under consideration. In both stablecoins and market-based finance, preserving access to cash and maintaining the value of assets under stress are separate questions. Ramsden offers a framework for where losses and liquidity demands could travel, without giving a trade or an estimate of individual issuer recoveries (pp. 12–15).

questions.question: How sensitive is the five-percentage-point capital benefit to the assumed cost of crises?
questions.detail: The FPC framework assigns a large role to resolution in reducing crisis severity, while the debt premium is evidence about creditor incentives. To test the capital conclusion, obtain the cited FPC assessment and Brooke et al. calibration and vary the frequency, duration and discounted output losses under successful and delayed resolution. The sensitivity matters for assessing whether a lower benchmark could survive a weak real-world execution.

questions.question: Which institutions actually save on funding after the change in transfer policy?
questions.detail: Figure 1 sets out indicative categories, but strategy remains firm-specific and some banks had already received decisions. Compare issuer-level resolution disclosures, MREL maturities, planned issuance and actual secondary spreads across firms with transfer and bail-in strategies. The cash-flow benefit depends on replacement funding costs and existing debt maturity. A change in classification does not itself determine the price of an outstanding subordinated bond.

questions.question: How would a rapid unwind of gilt repo affect an institution outside the backstop?
questions.detail: Chart 3 records growing net borrowing and the speech specifies which institutions can access the contingent facility. It does not quantify gross repo, haircuts, maturities or dealer balance-sheet capacity in stress. Examine the Bank's cited market data and exploratory scenario evidence alongside disclosures from financing counterparties. That would help identify whether additional market liquidity would reach a constrained borrower before forced selling transmits losses elsewhere.
